consensus_summary: “Year” has no single fixed symbolism; its broad figurative sense is a complete or divinely appointed period, commonly associated with Jubilee salvation, judgment, or prophetic chronology, while most occurrences remain ordinary calendar years.
book_summary: “Year” signifies a turning or complete cycle whose scale can vary; accordingly, the book reinterprets Jeremiah’s seventy years as seventy Jubilee-scale cycles and invokes Psalm 90 to support scale-relative time.
consensus_core_identification: A complete temporal cycle or appointed period whose particular symbolic force depends on context.
book_core_identification: One complete recurring cycle of time, applicable at any temporal scale.
boundary_disagreement: The book retains the consensus category of a complete temporal cycle but universalizes it across scales and reclassifies Jeremiah’s seventy years as seventy Jubilees. The consensus generally treats Jeremiah’s years as ordinary years and regards Jubilee, day-year, and other prophetic calculations as contextual alternatives rather than the intrinsic meaning of every “year.”
material_contradiction: There is no contradiction at the minimum core: both identify a year with a complete temporal period or cycle. The material disagreement concerns whether that cycle is inherently scale-variable and whether Jeremiah’s seventy years must be read as seventy Jubilees.
rationale: Because the book preserves the recognizable consensus identification of a complete cycle while materially expanding its scale and changing the classification of a major cited case, the relationship is REFINED rather than MATCH, DIVERGENT, or NOVEL.
strongest_objection: The printed texts mention seventy years, seventy weeks, and a thousand years being like a day to God, but none states that Jeremiah’s seventy years are seventy Jubilees. Psalm 90:4 is a comparison concerning divine temporal perspective, not by itself a rule allowing “year” to denote a complete cycle at any scale; the cited excerpts also do not establish the asserted Hebrew-root semantics.
